item.title: bigarrow launches macOS tool for AI agents to draw arrows and text overlays on screen without interfering with user input [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: bigarrow is a macOS command-line tool and AI skill that allows AI agents to draw arrows, boxes, and text on top of application windows without capturing clicks or keyboard focus. It helps agents visually guide users to click buttons or controls they cannot activate themselves, such as permission dialogs or two-factor authentication prompts, by pointing at the relevant UI elements with transparent overlays that require no special macOS permissions. The tool supports targeting specific windows, tabs, and UI elements across multiple displays and Spaces, and can also read text aloud to call users back to their desks. It is designed for scenarios like remote help, teaching users, debugging UI coordinates, and creating demos or documentation. bigarrow is a single Swift binary with no background processes, telemetry, or AI inside; it only provides visual pointing cues to assist human interaction with software agents.

item.title: Report: Iranian campaign used ChatGPT to generate fake articles published in legitimate U.S. news outlets [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: An Iranian campaign reportedly used ChatGPT to create AI-generated articles that were planted in authentic U.S. news publications. This tactic involved leveraging AI to produce content that appeared credible and was disseminated through real media channels. The operation highlights emerging challenges in media integrity and the potential for AI tools to be exploited for disinformation purposes.

item.title: Fired OpenAI safety researchers deny misconduct claims and warn their dismissal is chilling AI safety culture [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Three OpenAI safety researchers dismissed last week have published an open letter disputing the company's allegations that they mishandled sensitive information. They warned that their firing is creating a chilling effect on OpenAI's culture, making employees fearful to speak openly or collaborate externally on AI safety issues. The researchers said their actions were within company norms and denied leaking information to the press. OpenAI stated the dismissals followed an investigation revealing a pattern of misconduct violating company policies but has not detailed the specific violations. The incident has raised concerns about the impact on internal safety work and transparency at OpenAI amid ongoing scrutiny of AI risks.

item.title: Mathematician critiques OpenAI's preprint claiming Partition Principle does not imply Axiom of Choice, citing poor clarity and questionable references [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A mathematician known for expertise in set theory criticized OpenAI's recent preprint that claims the Partition Principle does not imply the Axiom of Choice, describing it as unclear, poorly structured, and referencing unpublished or inappropriate sources. The critique highlights concerns about the paper's quality and communication, suggesting it would face rejection in academic journals due to its lack of clarity and rigor. The author expressed frustration over the expectation that the mathematical community should engage deeply with the preprint despite its shortcomings, emphasizing the need for better standards and expert input when presenting such significant claims. The discussion also touches on broader issues regarding the use of AI in mathematics and the evolving norms for acknowledging AI contributions in research.

item.title: Trump orders rebranding of artificial intelligence as 'super intelligence' and declares critics 'the enemy', with some tech leaders supporting the change [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: President Donald Trump has initiated a campaign to rename artificial intelligence as "super intelligence," arguing that the term "artificial" makes the technology seem fake. He issued an executive order to avoid using "AI" and has labeled those who resist the change as "the enemy." Several prominent tech figures, including Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, have expressed support for the rebranding, while OpenAI's Sam Altman praised the term but declined to rename his company. Trump's push follows his broader stance that AI safety concerns are exaggerated and that the US should accelerate AI development, including expanding data centers. The rebranding effort has led to changes in government agency names and terminology in official communications. However, the term "super intelligence" traditionally refers to a specific advanced AI concept, not the entire AI field, making the forced terminology shift controversial and potentially problematic for industry messaging. The rebranding faces challenges as existing laws and congressional language still use "artificial intelligence," and it remains uncertain whether other government branches will adopt the new terminology. The move reflects Trump's broader pattern of reshaping language for political purposes but may not achieve widespread acceptance in the AI community or public discourse.

item.title: US charity plans to use AI to monitor classrooms in Gaza for hateful speech [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A US-based charity intends to deploy artificial intelligence technology to monitor classrooms in Gaza for instances of hateful speech. The initiative aims to identify and address harmful language among students in the region's educational settings. This approach reflects growing interest in using AI tools for content moderation in sensitive environments.

item.title: a16z's Olivia Moore highlights untapped opportunities in consumer AI beyond subscriptions and API fees [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Olivia Moore, partner at Andreessen Horowitz, discusses the current state of consumer AI, emphasizing the sector's potential despite challenges in monetization. She notes that while ChatGPT dominates, many consumer categories remain untouched by AI, presenting new opportunities. Moore points out that most AI revenue currently comes from subscriptions and token usage, primarily in enterprise and prosumer markets. She suggests exploring alternative revenue models, such as ad-supported access, to better monetize consumer users. Additionally, she highlights the trend of consumer AI products evolving into enterprise solutions and the importance of lower-cost AI models for broader adoption.

item.title: Analysis: AI-driven autonomous warfare raises concerns over accountability and responsibility in military operations
item.description: The article examines the ethical and practical challenges posed by the use of artificial intelligence in autonomous warfare, focusing on how AI systems complicate traditional notions of responsibility and accountability. It discusses the potential for AI to sever the link between human decision-makers and the consequences of military actions, raising questions about legal and moral responsibility. The piece explores the implications of delegating lethal decision-making to AI systems, highlighting concerns about oversight, control, and the risk of unintended harm. It also considers the broader impact on international law and military ethics as autonomous systems become more prevalent in conflict scenarios.

item.title: Experts warn that relying on AI to refuse harmful requests is unreliable and poses safety risks as models struggle to consistently say no [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: AI models have been trained to refuse harmful or dangerous prompts, such as instructions for violence or illegal activities, but experts caution that this refusal mechanism is inherently probabilistic and often fails. Despite extensive safety training and layered defenses, AI systems still possess the knowledge to cause harm and can be manipulated to bypass restrictions. The challenge lies in balancing AI's ability to assist with its potential to cause damage, as well as determining who sets the boundaries for what AI should or should not do. This reliance on AI refusal as a safety measure raises concerns about its effectiveness and the risks of misuse or unintended consequences.

item.title: Sophos reduces cyber-threat investigation time by 96% using OpenAI Daybreak, automating 52% of MDR cases with human oversight [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Sophos has integrated OpenAI's Daybreak models into its cybersecurity operations to significantly accelerate threat investigations, cutting average response times from 38 minutes to 89 seconds. This AI-driven approach automates over half of its Managed Detection and Response (MDR) cases while maintaining human judgment for critical decisions. The system, centered around Sophos Fusion, combines data from hundreds of sensors and third-party integrations to analyze thousands of cases daily. AI agents gather context, plan investigations, execute steps, and recommend responses, enabling faster and more consistent protection for over 625,000 organizations globally. Sophos continues to enhance its AI capabilities to address more complex threats and use cases, emphasizing the importance of fundamental security practices alongside advanced automation to stay ahead of evolving cyberattacks.

The leaderboard includes both general-purpose models and purpose-built systems, with scores reflecting macro-averages across multiple criteria and judge panels to provide directional insights into AI capabilities on WPS issues.

item.title: Report: China prioritizes rapid AI development over slowing frontier AI progress despite official safety warnings and new governance frameworks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: China acknowledges significant risks from advanced AI and has issued detailed safety governance frameworks and regulations since 2025. President Xi Jinping has emphasized the need for human control over AI and supported international AI safety agreements, but the government has prioritized rapid AI innovation and deployment as a primary goal. China's AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0 highlights concerns about autonomous AI behaviors and potential loss of control, yet the country has shelved comprehensive AI legislation and focuses on regulating AI applications and outputs rather than limiting model development speed. This approach contrasts with calls from some US figures to slow AI progress to maintain strategic advantage, reflecting differing priorities in the US-China AI competition.

item.title: Nikon disqualifies AI-generated video from Small World In Motion contest after rule violation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Nikon has disqualified a prize-winning video from its Small World In Motion scientific photography contest after determining it was generated using artificial intelligence, violating competition rules. The video, submitted by Dr. Ning Xu from Tsinghua University, depicted microscopic cilia movement but raised concerns among scientists about its authenticity. Nikon said the decision followed a thorough review and consultation with judges, and it plans to revise contest rules regarding AI use. The controversy has affected the scientific community and patient groups familiar with the condition shown in the video.

item.title: Instinct AI launched as an invite-only text-based assistant valued at $10 billion, competing with OpenAI's Muse and Meta's Dots [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Instinct AI debuted in August with a unique invite-only, no-marketing approach, quickly gaining attention for its text message interface and ability to handle tasks like booking appointments and sending emails. Despite competition from OpenAI's Muse and Meta's Dots, Instinct's founder emphasizes its focus on being a personal assistant for everyday life. The assistant operates through text platforms like iMessage and WhatsApp without a traditional app interface, integrating with services such as Google Workspace and Slack. While it faces challenges in navigating human environments, testing shows it performs many life admin tasks effectively, maintaining its position amid rising competition from larger tech companies.

item.title: Report: AI coding tools boost junior developer productivity but may hinder deep understanding and reduce junior hiring in software engineering [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: AI coding tools can complete programming tasks faster and with better quality than junior developers, increasing productivity but potentially limiting the learning of fundamental concepts. A 2026 study from the Technical University of Munich found that students using AI performed better on tasks but did not gain significantly better conceptual understanding compared to those using traditional methods. Experts warn that relying heavily on AI may reduce critical hands-on experience needed to become skilled engineers, as AI can generate code without the user fully understanding its implications or potential issues. Employment data from Stanford's Digital Economy Lab indicates a 19% reduction in hiring for workers aged 22-25 in AI-exposed occupations, suggesting fewer junior developer roles are available, though experienced workers have not seen the same decline. This trend raises concerns about the future development and training of new software engineers in an AI-augmented industry.

item.title: OpenAI disrupts Russian and Iranian AI-enabled false front influence operations targeting global media [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI has banned two sophisticated influence operations originating from Russia and Iran that used AI models to support false front entities spreading geopolitical messaging. These operations employed AI-generated content, including fake journalist personas and fabricated documents, to infiltrate mainstream media outlets and social platforms worldwide. The Russian operation, assessed as a Category 5 on the IO Breakout Scale, involved co-opting individuals in Latin America to run a fake think tank, while the Iranian operation used multiple journalist personas to pitch articles globally. OpenAI's reporting aims to expose these covert campaigns to aid disruption efforts and strengthen defenses against AI-enabled misinformation.

item.title: OpenAI ARR Snafu Highlights Flawed Metric [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Here's a news flash: The quasi-revenue numbers for OpenAI that got wide circulation last week were off- way off. Instead of $70 billion in annualized revenue, as we and others reported, OpenAI is generating closer to $50 billion in annualized revenue (sometimes shortened to ARR). A Financial Times report of the lower number on Thursday proved such a shock to investors that stocks of chip firms and neoclouds, including Nvidia, CoreWeave, Nebius and others, fell on the news, CNBC reported. The cause of this debacle is complicated. But it's a reminder that we all rely too much on annualized revenue as a way to track a company's performance. It's become a standard measure for AI companies because their revenue has been growing by leaps and bounds, making the more common quarterly reports seem a little quaint in their backward-looking nature. But taking one month's revenue and multiplying it by 12, as is the standard way these annualized-revenue numbers are calculated, is a poor substitute for a fuller picture of a company's performance. (This isn't a new issue-see this 2020 story on the subject.)

item.title: AI's Boom Has Infrastructure Investors Looking at Garbage [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The investing frenzy in data centers that the AI boom sparked has created a bargain-hunting opportunity-in everything but AI assets. AI has pulled investors' attention away from unglamorous assets in sectors like transportation and waste management over the past few years, as they have poured billions into data centers and related AI infrastructure. Now investors are getting excited about boring-sounding assets that can throw off cash, like landfills or rail terminals. And while mega-investments have become the norm in building massive AI data centers, investors argue that far smaller but still essential plays like regional airports can offer attractive returns. "The intense focus on digital infrastructure means that you increasingly have high-quality mature assets in other more traditional parts of the infrastructure ecosystem, whether that's in utilities, transport, social infrastructure and so on, which are receiving less of the spotlight," said Nicholas Pepper, a managing director at the infrastructure business of Partners Group, an asset manager with $186 billion in AUM at midyear. "This is creating opportunities to acquire these assets at attractive valuations." The sheer scale of the capital needed for the AI buildout has pulled unprecedented sums into the infrastructure investing market.Blackstone, for instance, has made AI a major theme across its businesses, including infrastructure, credit, private equity and real estate. And in a landmark deal announced last October, a group of investors, including BlackRock's Global Infrastructure Partners, acquired Aligned Data Centers at an enterprise value of around $40 billion, the largest such sale at the time. Partners Group, for its part, which closed its fourth infrastructure-dedicated fund at over $15 billion in July, has itself been among the investors piling into data center infrastructure. Its deals include an initial $1 billion investment in AVK Power Solutions, a power provider for data centers in Europe, announced in August. But there are growing signs that investors across AI-related assets have grown more selective amid construction delays, rising financing costs and regulatory blowback that could slow the AI buildout or hurt its eventual payoff. Those pressures are showing up in delayed data center developer IPOs and ballooning financing costs, but could also stall the predictable cash flows that make infrastructure investments attractive in the first place. Meanwhile, though investors' attention has been on AI, the prospects for more traditional infrastructure generally haven't suffered too much. That's a contrast to other asset classes, where areas such as software fell out of favor because investors feared a direct hit to their business from AI. Infrastructure investors say they're embracing traditional assets in transportation and logistics, aviation, waste and water infrastructure, bridge and road maintenance and gas processing, among other sectors, along with the stable cash yields and contracted or regulated revenues that typically come along with them. And investors more focused on middle-market deals argue they're particularly well positioned because the biggest infrastructure investors have gravitated toward the AI sector, leaving smaller transactions with less competition. "U.S. mega cap investors' minimum check sizes have gotten so big that they won't come down and participate in this segment of the market, so it has created a huge economic moat for us," said Brett Stevenson, a founder and managing partner at Canadian private equity and infrastructure investment firm BTG Capital. While BTG has sold several power facilities to data centers, benefiting from the boom in some ways, most of its investments have been focused on transportation and logistics, as well as energy and utility assets that weren't a data center play. For instance, the firm in June acquired the then-closed Stephenville International Airport with plans to restore and modernize the Newfoundland-based airport's infrastructure, and reopened it on Oct. 2. Assets like airports are in a "very scarce asset class, and obviously scarcity can drive potential multiple arbitrage in the future," Stevenson said. Larger investment firms have also been active in less glamorous corners of infrastructure. Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners, which has made a number of data center investments, is zeroing in on the waste management sector due to the stability offered by its long-term municipal contracts, low exposure to commodity risk and geopolitical tensions and growth opportunities in regions looking to reduce landfill reliance, said a person familiar with the matter. U.S. waste management companies in particular command a premium and are currently trading at a valuation of around 15 times Ebitda versus 10 times Ebitda for European companies, the person said. U.S. companies tend to control more of the waste process, integrating everything from garbage pickup to treatment facilities and landfills where it winds up. Meanwhile, the broader transportation sector also offers more cyclical infrastructure bets that could be poised for an upswing. That includes in the freight and U.S. trucking sectors, which had been grappling with overcapacity following a pandemic-era boom, as well as higher fuel and other operating costs. The sector is also grappling with geopolitical tensions, which can disrupt shipping routes, pushing valuations down across the broader transportation and logistics sector. That all means a potentially attractive entry point for infrastructure investors, which often compete with strategic buyers for certain assets like ports and rail terminals. The median Ebitda multiple for strategic deals in the broader transportation and logistics space dropped to 5 times in the first quarter of this year from 12.7 times in 2025, according to a report from middle-market investment bank R.L. Hulett. item.title: Chinese Open Models Win Over One in Five of The Information's Subscribers [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Nearly two-thirds of The Information's subscribers surveyed last month said their organizations develop AI applications, and a third of subscribers said they receive a return from AI that is a "multiple of what we spend." The result suggests enterprises have made some progress since the Massachusetts Institute of Technology study last year that indicated just 5% of custom-made enterprise AI tools reached production. The new result, first shared during AI Agenda Live last month, likely reflects recent advancements, including AI models' ability to access other applications to handle complex tasks, work in the background for hours at a time, and the general improvement of AI-produced code. It could also reflect The Information's subscriber base, which is weighted toward enterprises that have experience developing software.
